items.stem: The group associated with the excerpt above would NOT be expected to support which of the following views?
items.stimulus: “In the name of God, Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, etc. Having undertaken for the Glory of God and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honor of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the First Colony in the Northern Parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions and Offices from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience. In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names at Cape Cod, the 11th of November, in the year of the reign of our Sovereign Lord King James, of England, France and Ireland the eighteenth, and of Scotland the fifty-fourth. Anno Domini 1620.” Source: William Bradford, Mayflower Compact , 1646
options: (A) A strong desire to remove Catholic beliefs from the Anglican Church
(B) A commitment to the Calvinist principles of daily life
(C) A desire to establish a society of religious freedom
(D) A belief that governance should be derived from the will of the governed
items.explanation: Correct: (C). The excerpt is the Mayflower Compact (1620), in which the Pilgrims agreed to form a civil political body and to obey the laws it enacted — government by the consent of the governed, which supports (D). The signers were Puritans: Calvinists who sought to purify the Anglican Church of Catholic practices, supporting (A) and (B). But they sought religious freedom for themselves, not a society of religious freedom for others — the Puritan colonies were famously intolerant of dissent — so (C) is the view this group would NOT be expected to support.

option_explanations.A: The Pilgrims were Puritans who wanted to purify the Anglican Church of Catholic practices — they would support this view, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The Pilgrims were Calvinists whose daily life followed Calvinist principles — they would support this view, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Pilgrims sought religious freedom for themselves, not for others. Their colonies were famously intolerant of dissent — banishing Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson — so they would not support a society of religious freedom for all. This is the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Compact's 'civil body politic' founded on the signers' mutual covenant is government by consent of the governed — they would support this view, so it is not the exception.

items.stem: A continuity between the historical situation represented above and the First Great Awakening is that both were associated with
items.stimulus: “In the name of God, Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, etc. Having undertaken for the Glory of God and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honor of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the First Colony in the Northern Parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions and Offices from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience. In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names at Cape Cod, the 11th of November, in the year of the reign of our Sovereign Lord King James, of England, France and Ireland the eighteenth, and of Scotland the fifty-fourth. Anno Domini 1620.” Source: William Bradford, Mayflower Compact , 1646
options: (A) political activism in the early colonies
(B) philosophical enlightenment
(C) religious fervor
(D) increased commercialization
items.explanation: The First Great Awakening, a mid-18th-century wave of evangelical religious revival, saw a substantial return to the strong Calvinist doctrines of life and predeterminism. It saw a substantial return to the strong Calvinist doctrines of life and predeterminism. While political activism, (A), philosophical enlightenment, (B), and increased commercialization, (D), can be found at times throughout the colonies for much of this period, the First Great Awakening specifically pertains to this sudden and significant period of religious fervor in the colonies.

option_explanations.A: Political activism is not the thread linking the 1620 Compact to the 1740s revivals.
option_explanations.B: Philosophical enlightenment is not the link — the Awakening's emotional revivalism actually ran against cool rationalism.
option_explanations.C: Both were expressions of intense Protestant religious fervor: the Compact's godly mission to plant a Christian colony and the First Great Awakening's wave of revival and return to Calvinist doctrine.
option_explanations.D: Commercialization is not the thread connecting a 1620 religious covenant to an 18th-century revival.

items.stem: A historian could use this source to prove which of the following claims?
items.stimulus: “In the name of God, Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, etc. Having undertaken for the Glory of God and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honor of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the First Colony in the Northern Parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions and Offices from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience. In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names at Cape Cod, the 11th of November, in the year of the reign of our Sovereign Lord King James, of England, France and Ireland the eighteenth, and of Scotland the fifty-fourth. Anno Domini 1620.” Source: William Bradford, Mayflower Compact , 1646
options: (A) American colonists had already begun shedding their English identities as early as the 1600s.
(B) Religious and civil authority tended to intermingle in some English colonies.
(C) Religious freedom and tolerance were strong motivators for settlement in New England.
(D) The majority of the original settlers of Plymouth were Puritans.
items.explanation: Because the colonists in this document pledge loyalty to their “dread sovereign Lord King James,” it’s unlikely they were shedding their English identities, so eliminate (A). While we tend to associate the Puritans with religious freedom, “tolerance” was not a value they particularly cared about, so eliminate (C). For (D), there is no evidence in the source that the majority of the Plymouth settlers were Puritans, only the ones who signed this document (there were non-Puritans on the Mayflower too), removing (D). Choice (B) makes sense because the document shows how religion and government tended to overlap for these groups.

option_explanations.A: The signers pledge loyalty to their 'dread sovereign Lord King James,' so the document does not show colonists shedding English identity.
option_explanations.B: The Compact fuses a religious mission ('advancement of the Christian Faith') with civil government ('a civil body politic') — evidence that religious and civil authority intermingled in the colony.
option_explanations.C: 'Tolerance' was not a Puritan value; they sought freedom for themselves while punishing dissent, so the source does not prove tolerance motivated settlement.
option_explanations.D: The source shows only that the signers were Puritans. Many Mayflower passengers ('Strangers') were not, so it cannot prove the majority were.

items.stem: The revenue-generating measures imposed by the British in the mid-18th century were largely opposed by the colonists for all of the following reasons EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “Whereas by an Act made in the last session of Parliament, several duties were granted, continued, and appropriated, toward defraying the expenses of defending, protecting, and securing, the British Colonies and Plantations in America: and whereas it is just and necessary, that Provision be made for raising a further revenue within your Majesty’s Dominions in America, toward defraying the said expenses: We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, have therefore resolved to give and grant unto your Majesty the several rates and duties herein after mentioned.” Source: Stamp Act, 1765
options: (A) a lack of representation in British Parliament
(B) a perceived infringement upon the rights of the colonies to self-govern
(C) a post-war economic depression was already limiting economic growth in the colonies
(D) a desire to declare independence from Great Britain
items.explanation: During the mid-18th century (and even up to and during the Revolution), there remained a strong sense of loyalty toward the British. Very few at this time were calling for separation or independence, as hope remained for reform and greater representation in Parliament. The taxation and revenue-generating measures highlighted the lack of colonial representation in Parliament, (A), and interfered with the rights of the colonies to set their own taxes and self-govern, (B), both major points of contention among the colonies. In addition, the French and Indian War did lead to an economic depression, (C), which only exacerbated the impact of these new taxes and levies on the colonies.

option_explanations.A: Lack of representation — 'no taxation without representation' — was a genuine colonial grievance, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Perceived infringement on the colonies' right to tax themselves and self-govern was a genuine grievance, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: A postwar economic depression squeezing colonial growth was a genuine grievance, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: In the mid-1760s the colonists were still loyal Britons; very few wanted independence. They sought reform and representation within the empire, not separation — so this is the exception.

items.stem: The policy adopted by the Jefferson administration in response to the situation above most contradicted which of the following characteristics of the Democratic-Republican Party?
items.stimulus: “The cession of Louisiana and the Floridas by Spain to France works most sorely on the U.S. On this subject the Secretary of State has written to you fully. Yet I cannot forbear recurring to it personally, so deep is the impression it makes in my mind. It completely reverses all the political relations of the U.S. and will form a new epoch in our political course. Of all nations of any consideration France is the one which hitherto has offered the fewest points on which we could have any conflict of right, and the most points of a communion of interests…. There is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans, through which the produce of three-eighths of our territory must pass to market, and from its fertility it will long yield more than half of our whole produce and contain more than half our inhabitants. France placing herself in that door assumes to us the attitude of defiance.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, a letter written to U.S. Ambassador (to France) Robert Livingston, 1802
options: (A) A commitment to reducing the size of the military
(B) A belief in “strict construction” of the Constitution
(C) A preference for the interests of yeoman farmers
(D) A skepticism of government taxes and tariffs
items.explanation: Jefferson did not raise taxes or tariffs to pay for the Louisiana Purchase, so eliminate (D). Jefferson also did manage to reduce the size of the military while in office, so (A) can be eliminated too. Jefferson’s Louisiana Purchase added a significant amount of farmland to the American state, something welcomed by yeoman farmers, so eliminate (C). Choose (B) because Jefferson’s purchase of Louisiana was criticized by opponents who argued that he lacked the constitutional authority to make the deal with France (but it was too good of a deal for him to pass up).

option_explanations.A: Jefferson did reduce the size of the military in office; the Louisiana Purchase did not contradict that commitment.
option_explanations.B: Democratic-Republicans preached 'strict construction' — the federal government has only its listed powers. The Constitution says nothing about purchasing foreign territory, so Jefferson's sweeping purchase contradicted his own party's doctrine.
option_explanations.C: The purchase added vast farmland, delighting yeoman farmers — consistent with, not contradictory to, Democratic-Republican values.
option_explanations.D: Jefferson did not raise taxes or tariffs to pay for Louisiana — consistent with the party's skepticism of taxation.

items.stem: This excerpt would be most likely supported by
items.stimulus: “Sir, if you wish to avoid foreign commerce; give up all your prosperity. It is the thing protected, not the instrument of protection, that involves you in war. Commerce engenders collision, collision war, and war, the argument supposes, leads to despotism. Would the councils of that statesman be deemed who would recommend that the nation should be unarmed—that in the art of war, the material spirit, and martial exercises, should be prohibited…and that the great body of the people should be taught that the national happiness was to be found in perpetual peace alone? No, sir.” Source: Henry Clay, a speech in the House of Representatives, 1812
options: (A) the Federalists
(B) the War Hawks
(C) the British
(D) the French
items.explanation: Henry Clay was a noted War Hawk and his sentiments to go to war to protect foreign commerce were a common stance of fellow War Hawks. Federalists, (A), were opposed to war with Great Britain. Neither the British, (C), nor the French, (D), wanted the United States to continue to develop its military.

option_explanations.A: The Federalists opposed war with Great Britain; Clay's call to defend commerce by force was aimed against their position.
option_explanations.B: Henry Clay was a leading War Hawk. His argument — that abandoning commerce means abandoning prosperity, so the nation must arm and fight — was the War Hawks' case for the War of 1812.
option_explanations.C: Britain did not want the United States developing its military to use against Britain.
option_explanations.D: France did not want an American military buildup either, and France was not the power Clay was confronting.

items.stem: The conflict referenced in the speech above led to which of the following?
items.stimulus: “Sir, if you wish to avoid foreign commerce; give up all your prosperity. It is the thing protected, not the instrument of protection, that involves you in war. Commerce engenders collision, collision war, and war, the argument supposes, leads to despotism. Would the councils of that statesman be deemed who would recommend that the nation should be unarmed—that in the art of war, the material spirit, and martial exercises, should be prohibited…and that the great body of the people should be taught that the national happiness was to be found in perpetual peace alone? No, sir.” Source: Henry Clay, a speech in the House of Representatives, 1812
options: (A) The downfall of the Federalist Party
(B) Greater dependence on trade with Great Britain and France
(C) An increase in American territory
(D) The Monroe Doctrine
items.explanation: The Federalists were largely against the War of 1812 and felt that open war with Great Britain would stifle foreign trade and commerce. Ultimately, the War of 1812 led to fervent nationalism and the downfall of the opposition Federalist Party. As a result of the war, the United States saw a massive boost in domestic manufacturing due to lessened trade with Britain and France, so eliminate (B). The war did not directly lead to an increase in American territorial possessions, (C), nor did it directly lead to the Monroe Doctrine, (D).

option_explanations.A: Federalist opposition to the War of 1812 — culminating in the Hartford Convention — looked unpatriotic amid postwar nationalism, destroying the party. The war's most direct political consequence was the Federalists' downfall.
option_explanations.B: The war lessened dependence on British and French trade and spurred domestic manufacturing — the opposite of greater dependence.
option_explanations.C: The War of 1812 did not directly increase American territory; its gains were political and economic, not territorial.
option_explanations.D: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) came nearly a decade later and was not a direct product of the war.

items.stem: The speech above was most likely intended to criticize
items.stimulus: “Sir, if you wish to avoid foreign commerce; give up all your prosperity. It is the thing protected, not the instrument of protection, that involves you in war. Commerce engenders collision, collision war, and war, the argument supposes, leads to despotism. Would the councils of that statesman be deemed who would recommend that the nation should be unarmed—that in the art of war, the material spirit, and martial exercises, should be prohibited…and that the great body of the people should be taught that the national happiness was to be found in perpetual peace alone? No, sir.” Source: Henry Clay, a speech in the House of Representatives, 1812
options: (A) restrictions on immigration and laws intended to root out sedition
(B) limits on trade with France and Britain
(C) calls to end the international slave trade
(D) American support for France after the Haitian Revolution
items.explanation: Choice (A) is likely referring to the Alien and Sedition Acts, which is more of a policy from Adams’ time, so not relevant here. While the United States had just outlawed the international slave trade a few years before this, it’s not likely Clay had that in mind when writing this. Because this is in reference to a conflict with Britain, (D) is likely not relevant either. Choose (B) because this was written right around the time of the Embargo and Non-Intercourse Acts, heavily criticized by people like Clay who preferred war with Britain.

option_explanations.A: Restrictions on immigration and sedition refer to the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, under Adams — not relevant to Clay's 1812 speech on commerce.
option_explanations.B: Clay defends foreign commerce against those who would abandon it — a criticism of the Embargo and Non-Intercourse Acts that strangled American trade with France and Britain.
option_explanations.C: The 1807 ban on the international slave trade is not Clay's subject; his speech is about commerce and war with Britain.
option_explanations.D: American policy toward France after the Haitian Revolution is not the speech's topic; the conflict Clay addresses is with Britain.

items.stem: The political situation highlighted in the excerpt above is most similar to which of the following?
items.stimulus: “Mr. Adams is the Constitutional President and as such I would myself be the last man in the Commonwealth to oppose him upon any other ground than that of principle…. As to his character also, it is hardly necessary for me to observe, that I had esteemed him as a virtuous, able and honest man; and when rumor was stamping the sudden union of his and the friends of Mr. Clay with intrigue, barter and bargain I did not, nay, I could not believe that Mr. Adams participated in a management deserving such epithets…. But when these strange rumors became facts, when the predicted stipulation was promptly fulfilled, and Mr. Clay was Secretary of State, the inference was irresistible—I could not doubt the facts. It was well known that during the canvass Mr. Clay had denounced him as an apostate, as one of the most dangerous men in the union, and the last man in it that ought to be brought into the executive chair.” Source: Andrew Jackson, in a letter to Henry Lee, 1825
options: (A) The election of 1800
(B) The election of 1860
(C) The election of 1876
(D) The election of 1896
items.explanation: Here, Jackson is referring to the “Corrupt Bargain” between Adams and Clay that settled the presidential election of 1824. Find another example of an election that was resolved under similar circumstances. While the election of 1860 was certainly contested (it led to a Civil War), there was no bargain to be had there, so eliminate (B). The election of 1896 might have been perceived as corrupt by Populists bitter at Bryan’s loss, but again, there was no deal-making for that one and McKinley won fair and square. Jefferson’s “Revolution of 1800” saw a peaceful transfer of power in 1800 but no compromise. Choose (C), the election of 1876, because this was the election that ended Reconstruction over a bargain in Congress that made Hayes president.

option_explanations.A: The election of 1800 was also settled in the House (the Jefferson-Burr tie), but there was no corrupt bargain — no deal trading votes for office.
option_explanations.B: The election of 1860 involved no bargain; Lincoln won the Electoral College outright, and the result led to secession, not deal-making.
option_explanations.C: Like 1824, the election of 1876 was settled by a backroom deal: the Compromise of 1877 awarded Hayes the presidency in exchange for ending Reconstruction — the closest parallel to the Adams-Clay 'corrupt bargain.'
option_explanations.D: In 1896 McKinley won outright; Populists bitter over Bryan's loss cried foul, but there was no deal trading the presidency.
